senses: To plunge suddenly into water; to duck; to immerse.
To fall suddenly into water.
To put out; to extinguish.
ety: Probably of North Germanic origin, related to Swedish dunsa (“to plumb down, fall clumsily”), Danish dunse (“to thump”). Compare Old English dwǣsċan (“to extinguish”) and douse below.
examples: Set fire to your matches! / Douse them in gasoline!
The man who doused the fire was told to put the remainder of the coal into the bucket and then give the bucket to the soldier.
Once you feel confident in your visualizations, you may douse the candle by blowing it out.

senses: A genre of film or television that lies somewhere between drama and comedy.
A film or television programme belonging to this genre.
ety: Blend of drama + comedy.
examples: Last year, the Daily Mail found that Emily in Paris, a bubblegum dramedy starring Lily Collins, plugged 37 brands throughout 10 episodes.

senses: Someone who wipes.
Something, such as a towel, that is used for wiping.
Something, such as a windscreen wiper, that is designed for wiping.
A movable electric contact in some devices.
ety: From wipe + -er.
examples: So, Willy, let you and me be wipers / Of scores out with all men — especially pipers!
Using her hands like windshield wipers, she tried to flick snow away from her mouth. When she clawed at her chest and neck, the crumbs maddeningly slid back onto her face. She grew claustrophobic.

senses: A black female.
ety: From French négresse, from nègre. Equivalent to Negro + -ess.
examples: Hardly anywhere in the world will you find a negress driving a car. A negress acting as a chauffeur is still more extraordinary. Barely conceivable even in Harlem, but that was certainly where the car was from.

senses: Conventionalized.
Imitative; unoriginal; trite.
ety: From formula + -ic.
examples: Homeric Greeks valued clichés because not only the poets but the entire oral noetic world or thought world relied upon the formulaic constitution of thought.
That TV series has become awfully formulaic in the last couple of seasons.
Neoimpressionism quickly divided viewers: did it herald an abstract future or was it a dry, formulaic dead end?

senses: Within the nose.
ety: From intra- + nasal.
examples: As to the question of hay fever and asthma, intranasal disease is not the cause of every case of these two diseases.
The functioning of these nontaste and nonolfactory sensory systems in oral and intranasal stimulation is the subject of a recent volume.

senses: With a stomach stuffed full of food.
With the neck collared or encircled by an object.
Having a gorge or throat.
ety: From gorge + -ed.
examples: Gorged nearly to the uttermost when he entered the restaurant, the smell of food had almost caused him to lose his honor as a gentleman, but he rallied like a true knight.

senses: A holder of any of various offices in various (usually Islamic) countries, usually some sort of councillor.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi दीवान (dīvān), from Classical Persian دیوَان (dēwān), from Middle Persian dywʾn' (dēwān). Doublet of divan and douane.
examples: On these occasions I often heard him declare that the whole of Europe did not contain ten thousand men, and that as for King George, he was only fit to be a dewan or zamindar under himself.

Inviting himself and his dewan and his chamberlain to dinner with the Governor and Councillors in the Fort, he was received with imposing honours, and was feasted in the Council Chamber at a magnificent banquet.

senses: A lariat or lasso.
ety: From Spanish reata, from reatar (“to retie”). Compare lariat.
examples: A few blocks from the capitol we stripped him, cut off everything hanging between his legs, then fixed him with a riata and dragged him up and down Congress.

senses: A group of seven musicians.
A composition for a group of seven musicians.
A set of seven lines.
ety: From Latin septem (“seven”).
examples: The Lindsey Septet performs at Carnegie Hall this evening.
The K-pop septet BTS will return in spring 2026 with a new album and world tour.

senses: A maker of spurs.
ety: From Middle English sporiere; equivalent to spur + -ier.
examples: Gods so; my Spurrier! put 'em on Boy, quickly

senses: Any of several sorts of ice-cream flavoured with rum or sherry, often containing chopped cherries and topped with almonds, crumbled macaroons, etc.
ety: Borrowed from the Italian surname Tortoni; the dessert is usually regarded as named after Giuseppe Tortoni, a native of Naples, Italy, who was the proprietor of the famous Café Tortoni in Paris, France, in the early 19th century.
examples: With my own fair hands I've made individual almond tortonis for dessert. Cook thinks I'm a wonder! Each masterpiece in a fluted silver dish, silver candies sprinkled on the pink whipped cream! O-oh!
A big smile from the courtly waiter named Frank at Dominick's, an Italian restaurant in the Bronx. Huge hamburger steaks. Little tortoni in paper cups, vanilla ice cream topped with macaroon crumbs.

senses: A net or web; something structured or interlinked in a weblike manner.
ety: From web + work.
examples: Most frequently, the three make up the webwork of his literary fabric.
Very quickly it becomes evident that these webworks are part of an unaccountably large lair of thousands of spiders.
In some sense, the entire webwork of space-time would dissolve into myriad unconnected points in the spaceless and timeless Void with no communication between them.

senses: The first part of a play, in which the setting and characters are introduced.
ety: From Late Latin protasis, from Ancient Greek πρότασις (prótasis), from προτείνω (proteínō, “put forward, tender, propose”), from πρό (pró) + τείνω (teínō, “stretch”).
examples: It doubles itself in the middle of his life, reflects itself in another, repeats itself, protasis, epitasis, catastasis, catastrophe.

senses: The nocturnal, insectivorous, burrowing mammal Orycteropus afer, of the order Tubulidentata and somewhat resembling a pig. Common in some parts of sub-Saharan Africa.
ety: Borrowed from Afrikaans aardvark (now rare), erdvark, from aarde (“earth”, from Middle Dutch aerde) + vark (“pig”, from Middle Dutch varken). Early European colonists in South Africa noticed that the animal was similar to a pig, while aarde hints at the animal's habit of burrowing.
examples: The aardvark burrows in the ground and feeds mostly on termites, which it catches with its long, slimy tongue.
If ‘aardvark lover’ has that syntactic structure, then it determinately means “lover of aardvarks.

senses: A logical fallacy where criticisms are deflected by raising unrelated criticisms of the opposite side.
ety: From what about + -ism. First use appears c. 1978 in The Guardian.
examples: Soviet propagandists during the cold war were trained in a tactic that their western interlocutors nicknamed 'whataboutism'.
There's another attitude ... that many Russians seem to share, what used to be called in the Soviet Union 'whataboutism,' in other words, 'who are you to call the kettle black?'
This particular brand of changing the subject is called 'whataboutism' — a simple rhetorical tactic heavily used by the Soviet Union and, later, Russia.

senses: In blazon, coloured with a heraldic fur of a black field with white spots; counter-ermine.
ety: Attested in this form (with s) since at least 1562, in Legh's Accedens of Armorie, which defines it ("Sable poudred with Argent, … Ermines is his proper name") and contrasts it with both ermine and erminois. Related to ermine, but the derivation is unclear; the OED suggests "possibly [from] OF. herminès, pl. of herminet" (a supposed diminutive of hermine); modern French calls the fur contre-hermine. The Fifteenth Century Book of Arms (c. 1460) uses ermyne in a way that sometimes contrasts with ermyn (“ermine”) ("John Garther beryth of ix pecys ermyñ and ermyne"); The Ancestor says the image of
examples: He beareth Or, a Cheuron Checkey Ermin & Ermines.

senses: A grievance complained of.
A document sent by the Lower House of Convocation to the Upper House to inform the latter of certain grievances in the church.
The essence or ground of a complaint.
The essence or most important aspect of a piece of writing, a point of argument, etc.; the gist.
ety: Learned borrowing from Late Latin gravāmen (“physical inconvenience”) and Medieval Latin gravāmen (“grievance”), from Latin gravāre + -men (suffix forming neuter nouns of the third declension). Gravāre is the present active infinitive of gravō (“to burden, weigh down; to oppress”), from gravis (“heavy; grave, serious; hard, troublesome”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *gʷreh₂- (“heavy”)) + -ō (suffix forming regular first-conjugation verbs). The plural form gravamina is derived from Late Latin gravāmina.
examples: In 1239, the bishops presented gravamina to the papal legate detailing 'prejudices of ecclesiastical liberty by the lord king and his bailiffs'.
Falsehood, which was in ordinary cases the gravamen of the complaint, was omitted altogether in the information against him.
As we all know, Harry’s gravamen, the nub of his incandescent fury, is how he and Meghan were sold out by the institution.

senses: The idea that all of humanity belongs to a single moral community.
Transnationalism.
ety: From cosmopolitan + -ism. The sense referring obliquely to Jewishness comes from the long era in which all Jews lived in the Jewish diaspora because Jews had been banished from the ancient Jewish homeland and no new homeland yet existed. In Soviet use it was rooted in fear of transnationalism generally but took on coded or dogwhistle antisemitic qualities that were not explicitly separable from the generality.
examples: To present the world anthropologies project (WA), this article explores the existence of three kinds of anthropological cosmopolitanisms and cosmopolitics: imperial, liberal, and radical.

senses: A sudden heavy downpour of rain.
A sudden increase or rush of something; a flood, an outburst, an outpouring.
ety: The noun is derived from Middle English spate, spait (“a flood”), influenced by Scots spate (“torrent of water, flood; heavy downpour of rain; (figurative) bout of drinking; large crowd of people; flood of events, words, etc.”). The further etymology of the Middle English and Scots words is uncertain; they are possibly related to English spatter and Dutch spatten (“to spatter, splash”), possibly ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *sp(y)ēw-, *spyū- (whence English spit (“to evacuate (saliva or another substance) from the mouth, etc.”)), which is imitative of spitting. The verb is derived from
examples: Doun comes a jaw o' droukin' rain / Upon their honours— / God sends a spate outower the plain, / Or mebbe thun'ers.
Here is a fine spate of work—a day diddled away, and nothing to show for it!
He couldnae weel tell how—maybe it was the cauld to his feet—but it cam' in upon him wi' a spate that there was some connection between thir twa, an' that either or baith o' them were bogles.

senses: A representation of the sacred asp, symbolising supreme power in ancient Egypt.
ety: From Latin uraeus, from Ancient Greek οὐραῖος (ouraîos). This is traditionally assumed to be from Egyptian jꜥrt (“cobra in threat posture”), i-a:r:*t-I12, from jꜥr (“to rise, climb”); however, on phonetic grounds, Gundacker, following Fecht, argues for an origin in Egyptian wrrt (“White Crown, uraeus”, literally “the great one”) instead.
examples: In the small chamber opposite are Isis and Selket, and Nefertari's cartouche between two uraeuses.

senses: severe or intense
ety: From Middle English gnawynge; equivalent to gnaw + -ing.
examples: Engleitner found the constant gnawing hunger harder and harder to bear. When the rations eventually increased again and the prisoners were given stew, it did not make much difference to Engleitner.

senses: A collection or compendium, especially of coins or antiquarian objects.
A summary or digest of such a collection.
ety: From Ancient Greek συλλογή (sullogḗ), from συλλέγω (sullégō, “collect”).
examples: Ciriaco's epigraphic collections on paper, known as sylloges, are his most famous contribution.

senses: Of, related to or connected with syntax.
Containing morphemes that are combined in the same order as they would be if they were separate words e.g. greenfinch
ety: From New Latin syntacticus, from Ancient Greek συντακτικός (suntaktikós).
examples: The sentence “I saw he” contains a syntactic mistake.

senses: A Chinese crescent-shaped dumpling filled with a minced stuffing and steamed, boiled or fried; the Chinese originator or predecessor of the Japanese gyoza.
ety: From the Hanyu Pinyin romanization of the Mandarin Chinese pronunciation for 餃子／饺子 (jiǎozi). Doublet of gyoza.
examples: I took the Blakes over for a jiaozi dinner in the park—not my favorite place although the jiaozis were much better than the food we had before.
Jiaozi are eaten all year long and at any time of day—breakfast, lunch, or dinner.

senses: A person who sometimes wears clothes traditionally worn by and associated with the opposite sex; typically a male who cross-dresses occasionally by habit or personal choice.
ety: Borrowed from Latin trāns + vestītus, form of vestiō (“to clothe, to dress”) (as in English vestment, vest). Literally, a "cross-dresser". From transvestitism, from German Transvestitismus, coined in 1910 by Magnus Hirschfeld (the practice itself is much older).
examples: Even though Steven used to dress up in his sister's clothes, it still came as a surprise he ended up as a transvestite.
Now, we already know that Gerald Hadleigh was a transvestite or a transsexual, whatever the term is.

senses: To lessen in price or estimated value; to lower the worth of.
To decline in value over time.
To belittle or disparage.
ety: Inherited from Middle English depreciaten, borrowed from Late Latin dēpretiātus / dēpreciātus, perfect passive participle of dēpretiō / dēpreciō (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- + pretium (“price”) + -ō.
examples: To prove that the Americans ought not to be free, we are obliged to depreciate the value of freedom itself.
They depreciated him because he was the youngest on the team.

senses: mezzo-soprano
ety: (music): Clipping of mezzo-soprano
examples: Emily Golden, a mezzo who was adept in an especially wide range of roles;

senses: Someone who cuts up; someone who acts boisterously or clownishly, for example, by playing practical jokes.
A work produced by the aleatory literary technique of cutting up and rearranging a written text to create a new text.
ety: Deverbal from cut up.
examples: Although Dek can be a cutup, his explanation for his obsessive search for the truth — “It was about respect” — reveals the bedrock of decency that makes him a seriously good guy.

senses: Arousing or intensifying sexual desire.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀφροδισιακός (aphrodisiakós, “venereal”), from Ἀφροδίσιος (Aphrodísios, “pertaining to Aphrodite”).
examples: Cognac, with the addition of a little paprika and the yolk of an egg, is considered an effective aphrodisiac aid.

senses: Placing humans at the center of something, giving preference to humans above all other considerations.
ety: From anthropo- + -centric.
examples: But just as we recognize that nature doesn't provide a very good guide for human social conduct, isn't it anthropocentric of us to assume that our moral system offers an adequate guide for what should happen in nature?

senses: A group of people crowded or gathered closely together.
A group of things; a host or swarm.
ety: From Middle English throng, thrang, from Old English þrang, ġeþrang (“crowd, press, tumult”), from Proto-Germanic *þrangwą, *þrangwō (“throng”), from *þrangwaz (“pressing, narrow”), from *þrinhwaną (“to press, to push; to force”), from Proto-Indo-European *trenkʷ- (“to beat; pound; hew; press”). Cognate with Dutch drang, German Drang. Compare also German Gedränge (“throng”) and Persian ترنجیدن (Trenjidan, “to beat, to push”). Compare typologically crowd (see there for more).
examples: Not to know me argues yourselves unknown, The lowest of your throng.
Perhaps you suppose this throng / Can't keep it up all day long?
I imagine throngs of people – well-dressed, sipping spritzes – in front of a boat that, to me, is a coffin which held 700 people.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of a drum.
Of a tile, producing a drum-like sound when tapped or walked on because there is a hollow area beneath.
ety: From drum + -y.
examples: Water dripped onto the tarpaulin with a drummy sound.

senses: To use GPS or other data to provide map coordinates to a person, an object, or event.
ety: From geo- + locate.
examples: We have geolocated the missing ship, so we can now send rescue personnel.
He geolocated the video using a database of millions of images from around the globe, and it pointed to a street in Minab, Iran, several hundred feet from an elementary school.

senses: Of or characteristic of sisters.
ety: From sister + -ly (adjectival suffix).
examples: Burton designed both Middleton sisters' dresses in white, so that when Pippa picked up Kate's train in the abbey, the two of them were united, visually, in a display of sisterly togetherness.

senses: To make quiet.
To become quiet.
ety: From quiet + -en (verbal suffix).
examples: Take deep, deep breaths and quieten your mind while you contemplate what has been revealed within my latest journallings to you.

senses: Master; sir: a title used in the Middle Ages, given to a person in authority, or to one having a licence from a university to teach philosophy and the liberal arts.
The possessor of a master's degree.
The chief male celebrant of an occult ritual.
ety: Borrowed from Latin magister (“a master, chief, head, superior, director, teacher, etc.”), from magis (“more or great”) + -ter. Doublet of maestro, master, and meister.
examples: If only the Magistra and Magister of the Rite are present, then just the Magister shall drink of simulate if fake (ie theatrical) blood is used.
Just as there are tools and symbols that are specific to the Magistra, the stang is a tool used to represent the Horned God and should be used by the Magister only.
Fourth Degrees migrate, Magistras & Magisters administering.

senses: The scientific study of death and the practices associated with it, including the study of the needs of the terminally ill and their families.
ety: From thanato- + -logy, from Ancient Greek θάνατος (thánatos, “death”).
examples: The work is part of a growing field called comparative thanatology — the study of how different animals react to death.

senses: A pig, especially a castrated male, being fattened and raised for slaughter.
ety: From pork + -er. * (obese person; police officer): Carried over from the same senses of pig. * (a lie): Extension of the rhyming slang pork pie.
examples: Jerry Lynch, a pig's head pickled. Term usually applied to the long Irish heads which are sent over here for sale in the poorer districts of London, and which are vastly different from the heads of “dairy-fed” porkers.
All the other male pigs on the farm were porkers.

senses: A French baroness.
ety: Borrowed from French baronne.
examples: The murderer had forced the baronne into a compromising correspondence, enlisted his friends as allies in the epistolary exchange, and displayed her signature to imply her consent.
